ResponsesInList.Title: Moving a discussion to a different course
ResponsesInList.Text: I know you can move a discussion to a new forum within the same course. But, is it possible to move a discussion to a different course?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moving a discussion to a different course
ResponsesInList.Text: You can move a whole forum to another course, using the backup and restore functions. You use "Backup" in the admin block of the course where the forum presently is. You then use the "Restore" link *in that same course* - you get to choose the destination course ... These instructions are for Moodle 1.8.4 / 1.8.2 First, you backup only the forum (the forum you want to move). To do this, you first click "Backup" in the admin block (of the course presently containing the forum). click "Backup" in the admin block. You should now have a list of check boxes of things you can backup from that course. next to "Include", click "None". look down the list and identify the forum you want to copy tick the forum you want to copy, and tick "User Data" immediately to it's right. scroll down the page, and next to "Metacourse" dropdown select No. (I'm not sure if this has any effect, but I'm guessing this is the right setting. click Continue In the Name field, give the zipfile a name that you will easily recoginse - like ForumToMove.zip Click Continue. You'll now get a page showing the backup file being created, and at the end of the page will appear a Continue button. click Continue. You'll be taken to a page listing all the backup files for that course. Stay in this page. Next, you copy the forum to where you want it to go to, using the "Restore" function.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: The meaning of the star?
ResponsesInList.Text: Floyd, I hear what you are saying about ranking, etc., but after reading hundreds of Martin messages, I can't believe he has any kind of social notion tied up with this (that would be very anti- constructionist ). I think he is testing out group implementation at moodle.org, just like he has tested everything else out here, too. I know that when I use groups in Moodle, it will be because I have one course with three sections of students. While the forums will continue to involve everyone in my course, it will be much easier for me to respond to one group of journals and assignments, etc. at a time. In classes where professors lecture to a large group (and have assistants to help with running break-out sessions), this feature will help break-down the activities and responsibilities accordingly. Since moodle.org doesn't really have a parallel structure to that kind of academic classroom (or at least a parallel that we have envisioned yet), I suspect Martin was looking for a quick way to draw a moving line (and he chose something like frequency and focus). I am grateful the line wasn't drawn because of nationality (I love the growing diversity of voices and experiences here), because of coding prowess (I have none), because of discipline (how many 11th grade lit teachers are in this community?), or because of Moodle vision (or lack thereof--see my aborted library add-on idea). IMHO , it seems like we're all here to learn from each other and there really aren't any borders or fastened lines. best, Tom

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: The meaning of the star/hat?
ResponsesInList.Text:
What a fascinating discussion to wake up to - thanks everyone! The hats were only intended to reward behaviours which I, as
facilitator, am trying to promote in these Using Moodle forums (because they are beneficial to the community in general). It's meant to recognise people who stand out as being particularly connected and helpful ( which is not necessarily the same as people who post a lot in a well-intentioned way ). The idea was mostly to help newcomers to identify role models . No ranking was intended. Unfortunately, because the forums
are so connected with Moodle development the hats can easily be tied
up with all sorts of other meanings. The star (which was an education joke to start with) was not a good choice, and even the hat is a powerful symbol. I never anticipated how strongly that would affect the look of the forums. I think on balance any sort of symbol that separates people in this course will probably cause more trouble than they solve, but I'll make a few of my observations from the past few days: Positive: Those with hats are proud to have the recognition Many of those with hats have been trying a little harder recently to live up to their "status" Some feel fairly passionate about it Some people without hats seem to be trying a little harder (to get one?) Negative: People without hats can feel like they are missing out on something To me this indicates that applying symbols to groups within a classroom (much like logos, or military ranks, or grafitti tags) can have a lot of potential to stir up emotion, discussion and role-playing. Applied properly this looks like a very powerful tool for facilitating and guiding class interaction. I'm looking forward to more experimentation with all this once 1.2 is released! In the meantime, I'll guess I should remove the symbol from that group (sorry, hat guys! ). Note there has been another new feature recently, which is that forum ratings can now be public (and have been made so for most of these forums) so perhaps we can use that as a more immediate and democratic way of rating participation here.

I liked that a new Moodler may look to me for an answer if there weren't any smart people around at the time. I liked my hat. Hats are good. They tell us something about the wearer. I think the mortarboard, as a symbol for Moodle, was a flash of genius. This is a learning place for people working to build and use learning software. We can all ask for help and we can all offer help. Some help more than others. Many would help if they thought they could, many would love to help more than they do, many will help more when they learn more. Many will help when they've gained enough confidence. Those that can help, and then do help, will wear a mortarboard, although now, they will have to imagine it. And those looking for help will still get the answers they need, but then, they always did anyway. Symbols are important. Probably more so to the one looking for answers. I think there are many people here who should be recognized for their skills and many people who should be recognized for their willingness to help. I really think these people should be recognized because they combine the two and really do help people. People like me who are trying to learn how to use Moodle to help others but wouldn't have a chance without these generous people who are willing to share their experience and give their time to help. Hats off to you all, you know who you are. In closing, I was going to offer my hat to Timothy Takemoto for helping me to become more introspective than I've been in years. The guy says things and I go into this really deep introspective kinda place and have to re-examine my long-held philosophies and beliefs to see if they still work for me. Invariably they do still work for me but I seriously appreciate the provocation that provides this all too rare opportunity to think, I mean really think. Hats off to you too Tim, for saying what you think. Martin, please put the mortarboard back next to your picture. The buck has to stop somewhere. In here the buck stops there. Symbols are important, where would we be without them.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Allowing some users to create new topics in the Site News forum on the Front Page
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Peter, By defining the default front page role as student, users can participate in all student activities. However the site news forum is not considered a student activity, since everyone is forced to be subscribed and if students are able to post replies then this could result in tons of forum emails being generated. Anyway, if you want students to be able to reply in all news forums on your site, you can edit the role of student in Administration > Users > Permissions > Define roles and set the capability mod/forum:replynews to allow. If you only want students to be able to reply in the site news forum, as you've worked out, you can set a news forum role override. Users are not automatically assigned a front page role when they access the front page, so you do need to add each of your teachers as students. Multiple users may be selected by holding down the Apple or Ctrl key whilst clicking on the users' names. Regarding news forums elsewhere, when you create a course, a news forum is included in it automatically. Please see the news forum documentation for further information.

ResponsesInList.Title: Grading Options for Forum
ResponsesInList.Text: Hello -- I know this we discussed a while ago and there is some discussion of this topic in the bug tracker, but I am trying to determine if there is an easy way to start grading forums by cumulative points instead of by average. I know that some people have expressed that this is perhaps not educationally good because it promotes quantity over quality. However, the current system only promotes quality of one post and discourages extra discussion. When I rate the forum, I like to give every post a grade so that I know I read that post. So, if I student posts two good posts that get a 13/15 and a 14/15 but then just post a simple reply that I give a 0 to, then they end up with a 9/15 which is not a good grade. I would like to be able to set the maximum points at 15 and give a post a grade of like 5, so if a kid sends in 3 good posts, 4/15, 5/15. 4/15 they get a 13/15 which is more representative. I have seen a few patches for 1.9, but I would like to start doing this now. There is a way I saw where someone edited forums.php, but I don't have that power. Anyway, is there a way to accomplish what I am seeking via either some add-on or via a custom scale or some other method. I have installed the 1.9 beta 4 on an extra site, but I don't see an option in teh grade book or in the forum about this.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Grading Options for Forum
ResponsesInList.Text: Peter - I posted a patch that we are hoping to get into 1.9 shortly. It sounds as if you have already checked out the discussion at MDL-3942 . The patch should provide teachers with the ability to use sum, count, max, min, or average (the current default). I'm not sure what your time frame is but you may want to consider grading the forums and then updating the code once the changes get committed. Once you change to type of scoring, it should then recalculate the grades for that forum discussion. Peace - Anthony

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Grading Options for Forum
ResponsesInList.Text: Peter - The patch for MDL-3942 has been applied to the 19STABLE branch and HEAD which means if you get the latest version from CVS it will be in there. Peace - Anthony

ResponsesInList.Title: one forum for three courses????
ResponsesInList.Text: Is there a way to create one forum that can be used by students from three different courses?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: one forum for three courses????
ResponsesInList.Text: Chris, a Meta Course may be your best bet. The Parent course is the Meta Course, and the Child Courses can be "enrolled" into the Meta course. The students are automatically added to the Meta course since they are already in the Child Courses. Doug

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: one forum for three courses????
ResponsesInList.Text: Thanks, but how do I accomplish this?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: one forum for three courses????
ResponsesInList.Text: You need to get your administrator for Moodle to create a Meta Course with you as the teacher, and then add the courses in. Then you click on the Child Tab under the Admin block. Since I am admin for our server , I'm not sure if you can see the tab or you may have to get your Moodle admin to do it. Then you add the courses. Doug

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: one forum for three courses????
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Chris and Doug, The admin (or anyone with course creation privileges) should create a new course. In the course settings, set Is this a meta course = Yes. Don't assign a Teacher. Then click the Course administration block -> Child courses link and select the three courses that you want to be children of the metacourse. Put the forum in the metacourse. Here's another discussion almost identical to this one.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: one forum for three courses????
ResponsesInList.Text: Once you have the Metacourse created, you will need to setup the forum. If you want a single discussion forum for the members of all three child courses to have access, I would recommend that the metacourse be setup as a social format. To do that someone (the admin or a course creator) will need to go into the meta course and click on settings in the administrator toolbar. For "format" select "social format." Now this metacourse has become a discussion forum that anyone in the subscribed courses (child courses) will have access to. If you need multiple lines of discussion in this course I would set it up similar to the way this "Using Moodle" classroom is setup - "Topics Format" with as many topics and forums as you need. Good luck. If you get a chance, let us know what you ended up doing and how it turned out.

ResponsesInList.Title: Anonymity in Forums
ResponsesInList.Text: Is there a way to set up a forum (or other peer interactive activity, such as wiki or workshop) so that participants are anonymous?  In some discussions it would be helpful if the students didn't know whose post they are responding to or assessing, while also knowing that their own posts are anonymous (except to the teacher). If not, can one of you experienced Moodlers give me a rough idea about whether some kind of "Hide Identity" function would be a relatively easy mod or rather difficult? Thanks, Jim Robertson.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Anonymity in Forums
ResponsesInList.Text: It would be rather difficult, as Moodle is very much geared towards community, participation and understanding of other people. There are some plans around for a whole simulation / roleplaying module which would allow anonymous roleplaying but currently these are just plans.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Anonymity in Forums
ResponsesInList.Text: Thanks for the quick reply.   I have been amazed in following a few of these posts how rapidly an idea gets developed and explored once it's been brought up. Just to clarify, we don't wish to discourage community, participation, or understanding:  the intent of anonmymity in some forums is to encourage participation from those who might otherwise remain more in the background, and to put everyone on an equal footing by preveniting preconceived ideas about the value of a post based on the identity of the person posting. Thanks again, Jim Robertson.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Anonymity in Forums
ResponsesInList.Text: As someone who previously worked for a university and is currently involved in the delivery of education and training for a non-academic institution, I have learned that successful strategies for community building and participation take different forms. The use of an anonymity for posting forums is a good example. Ive had several instances where anonymous forums would have helped create a more open and participatory environment. Heres one example. A manager wanted to engage her staff (supervisors and clerks) in a discussion about job training strategies she is thinking of implementing. She thought that using an anonymous discussion forum would ensure that suggestions and ideas would be evaluated based on their own merits, without regard to the source of the ideas. Some might argue that the manager should have created an environment where her subordinates felt free to speak their minds without having to hide their identities. As it turns out, this person is an excellent manager with very good communication skills, but has a number of people working under her who because of cultural and other factors are reluctant to disagree with people in positions of authority. I can understand if there are technical issues that make it difficult to allow for the option to create anonymous posts. But educationally speaking, I think we need to trust that course creators have the wisdom to decide if and when anonymous postings are appropriate.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Anonymity in Forums
ResponsesInList.Text: Dear Eddie Davis > but has a number of people working under her who because of cultural > and other factors are reluctant to disagree with people in positions of > authority. Yes, this is the point. As a cultural psychologist living in Japan, I could not agree more. It is very easy when living in a Western, Christian, country, and even or especially a Western country where non-Westerners are expected to merge with Western values, to believe that discourse and disclosure are universally good. It is my belief that the Japanese self is not in the narrative but the 'imaginary' (that which can be imagined, recalled visually). Forcing Asians to identify with a narrative is a stressful double task that can get in the way. On the other hand here in Japan there is a great tradition of communication disclosure, called "getting together naked." Everyone gets together in a public bath with their kit off. This is one of the many community building methods that I would not recommend the Japanese attempt to export. There are things that do not export well. Have you tested the hack? I am still a little unsure about the email. Timothy

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Anonymity in Forums
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Timothy & Eddie, Thanks for the discussion on anonymity.  I believe it is valuable in Western culture as well.  It is not simply a case of preventing prejudicial judgements.  Adopting an "unknown" self can give a person the opportunity to explore responding in ways they might not otherwise discover.  Anonymity removes a person's normal social self and provides a context for trying out a different sort of self.  MediaMOO at MIT and similar MOO and MUD projects exploit that aspect of anonymity.  I have not participated in them, but this forum achieves much of what I would desire in an anonymous class forum: we don't have anonymity as such, but we define ourselves to each other by our questions and responses and are otherwise unknown to one another -- yet there is very much a sense of community here, as well as a high level of learning. Cheers, Jim.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Anonymity in Forums
ResponsesInList.Text: I come and look at this thread from time to time, since anonymity is a legal requirement and essential for group participation in my classes, and this statement above jumps out Martin Dougiamas writes: "as Moodle is very much geared towards community, participation and understanding of other people." ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Anonymity in Forums
ResponsesInList.Text: Dear Jim As Martin says, anonymity would not be easy to acheive, but of course it would not be impossible either. This is open source. It is possible to hack the code at your own, considerable, risk. I do something similar with my "help forum" which is on the top page of my site and open to guests and the whole wide world, to ensure that pictures are not displayed at the site level. To do this I changed the first line below (about line 1463) to the third line below. //    if ($picture) {  // Print custom user picture // Takemoto only teacher pics on front page . if ($picture && ($courseid > 1 || isteacher($courseid, $userid))) { This means that unless the "course id" is greater than one or the user is a teacher, then the default "smilely" picture will be displayed. The moodle site itself is course id = 1, so that this means that photos are displayed in courses proper but not on the front page. Here Japan, anonymity may be a way of encouraging people to post to forums (something Japanese seem to find very difficult to do), so I have looked into applying the same principle to the username. There is a function called "fullname" in moodle/lib/moodlelib.php which is responsible for sending back the name of the user to be used in all places where the username is printed on the screen. Unfortunately the course id is not passed to this function, so removing the name in particular courses is not as easy as removing the picture. But if you were to: 1) make a course for anonymous postings with id=2 or whatever 2) hack moodle/lib/moodlelib.php changing function fullname($user, $override=false) { to function fullname($user, $override=false, $mycourseid=3) { if ($mycourseid=2) { ....till the end of the function... else { return "Anonymous";} where 3 is NOT the id of the anonymous courses. 3) hack moodle/mod/forum/lib.php so that every time the function fullname() is called from the forum function library, the course id is passed as well.... then it does seem to be possible to ensure that all the names are displayed as "anonymous" on the "anonymous" course.  This is a little tricky because the variable containg the "course id" is called variously $course->id $courseid $course but it is by no means impossible. 4) This still leaves the link from the profile of the poster and this is more difficult to deal with since it is not created by any central function. Rather than change the forum module, it would be easier just to prevent students from seeing each other's profiles. To do this one could change moodle/user/view.php adding if (isteacher()){ ....till the end of the page... } else { echo "only teachers are allowed to view profiles"; } 5) The anonymous forums would be kept inside a particular course, or courses, into which students would have to enrol, or which could be a 'meta course'.  You would then have to link to the anonymous forums from each of your courses. This would mean that anonymous forums would be accessible from all those courses which are taking part (unless you created several anonymous courses). So, this would entail quite a lot of hacking to your site, including the central modules, entailing risk. The solution would only be partial, since the forums would be in one course (again, unless you created several anonymous courses). In order to make an "anonymous" type of forum, one would have to ensure that the forum type variable is passed to all the functions in the forum library, but at the moment this is not the case. So quite a lot of changes would have to be made. Alternatively, if you don't mind complete anonymity then you could change the language pack of your site so that students enter a pen name in first and second name fields and their real name into one of the fields that only the teachers can view in the user profile. Timothy

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Anonymity in Forums
ResponsesInList.Text: Dear Jim Robertson The attached zip file is an improperly tested hack for achieving semi-anonymous forums on moodle 1.4.4. If you were to try it out, then please back up the files, your course, and your database . Three files have been changed. 1) moodle/lib/moodlelib.php This is the main set of functions for moodle. I have added an extra variable which accepts the forum type in the function "fullname". If the forum type is single (all in one thread started by the teacher) then instead of returning the name of the student, the function returns "anonymous." Additionally the word "anonymous" is preceded by and followed by so that the link is now shown. It still exists however, so you would need to put userprofiles off limit to increase anonymity. But even then users who realised that the links are still inside the source would be able to tell who is posting what from the user id numbers of other, non anonymous forum posting. I hope that fullname is used to produce the link as well in future, and there is flag for turning it off. 2) moodle/mod/forum/lib.php All the functions that call "fullname" from forum lib.php have have been modified so as to pass the forum type, hide photos and pass the forum type to "fullname," above. It would be possible to acheive complete anonymity by editing this file so that links are not displayed. In this case there would be no need to adjust moodle/lib/moodlelib.php. 3) moodle/mod/forum/post.html Two lines have been modified again so as to pass the forum type. The forum type can be set in the usual way at the top of the forum set up screen. Single topic forums are still limited to a single topic started by the teacher, and they are anonymous. It would be easy to set the "anonymous" forum to any of the other types but it would be more difficult to add another type. The social forum type is rarely used (only on "social layout" courses) but this type cannot be set from the GUI (other than by creating a social layout course) but it can be set from the database. As it stands the teacher can't see who made the posts either. But grades are transmitted to the gradebook. Timothy

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Anonymity in Forums
ResponsesInList.Text: There was a mistake in the above (moodle/mod/forum/post.php was not correctly modified). ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Groups in the Forum module
ResponsesInList.Text: Andy, It sounds like you are doing this correctly, but you should check the setting for group visibility course-wide in the course settings (not the forum settings). Make sure that Force is set to No under the Groups section, otherwise it won't matter how you try to set up groups in the forum settings. You should have Separate groups selected in the forum settings. The Visibility toggle simply hides the entire forum from the students, so they don't see it at all until you want them to. If you want students to rate each others' posts, you can setup a custom rating scale for this and apply it to the forum. To allow students to access this, you will probably need to give them permission through a role override. In the forum settings, select the Roles tab at the top and then click Override roles (assuming you only want these settings for this particular forum). Click Student, then check the second column (Allow) next to Rate posts. Otherwise, only the teacher will be able to rate posts, if that's the default setting for the course. ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Not allowing students to create new topic
ResponsesInList.Text: Starting in Moodle 1.7, you must do this through the roles and capabilities system. First, you must get your Administrator to do two things: allow Teachers to override the Student role (Site administration -> Users -> Permissions -> Define roles -> Allow role overrides). override the Teacher role, allowing Teacher to "Override permissions for others." If your administrator wants to do this for ALL teachers, he can do it in the System context (Site administration -> Users -> Permissions -> Manage roles), but is safer to do it in some lower-level context, preferably in just your course. Now you must do this: Override the Student role in this particular forum (Click the forum, then click the Update button, then click the Override roles tab and edit the Student role, changing the capability "Start discussions" from Allow to Prevent. That's all there is to it

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Two Courses, One Forum?
ResponsesInList.Text: It's not a perfect solution, but you could do this with a metacourse. Create a new course and set "Is this course a metacourse" to Yes. ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Forum Ratings - Some Students Cannot Be Rated
ResponsesInList.Text: One thing that has created that situation for us is that the dates get set in the forum setup for "Restrict ratings to posts with dates in this range." Unfortunately, after those are set, it grays out and looks like it isn't set--making it hard to tell if it is set or not. So, take a look at the posting dates. Are the posting dates for students that do not have the rating dropdown before or after the dates of the students who do have the rating dropdown? If so, go into the forum and update it by checking the box beside "Restrict ratings to posts with dates in this range." Expand the dates listed to cover all the posting dates. Save. Then see if the rating dropdown appears. If it does, go back in and uncheck the box beside "Restrict ratings to posts with dates in this range" to turn it off. Bruce

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Site News - how to clear all messages?
ResponsesInList.Text: If it is a news forum that only allows posts (no replies), then you could go into the database and delete all posts to that forum. Just see what the forum number is...click on it and see the number in the browser. Then, (using phpmyadmin as an example) go into your database and open the mdl_forum_discussions table and sort by the "forum" column. Check each entry for the forum number of the news forum and drop them. Of course, you could run an sql querry to do the same thing. If there are replies to those posts, then it gets a little more complicated, since those replies will be in the mdl_fourm_posts table. Caveat...this is a theory...totally untested by me, but it "should" work. Use at your own risk and backup first Steve

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: How do I make it so forum members do not receive emails?
ResponsesInList.Text: My experience is that, while teachers say that they would “prefer to go to the forum” the reality is that, if they find deleting emails they should be monitoring too irksome, they’re unlikely to bother to go to the forum, which leaves it unmonitored, possibly for long periods. In a fair sized school one person cannot be responsible for monitoring all forums, and what a liberal teacher might feel acceptable in their forum another might find inappropriate, so each teacher really should accept responsibility for those forums he/she creates.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: How do I make it so forum members do not receive emails?
ResponsesInList.Text: The point is, you "go to to the forum" to read the responses instead of them "coming to you" via email. Otherwise, why not just have a listserv. I use Moodle in two different contexts. I have a Moodle site for my face to face courses and I am setting one up for a professional organization which currently uses listservs for about two thousand people. By having the e-mail come to my inbox, I am reminded to visit the forum. I check my e-mail regularly, a simple shift-command-T on my keyboard downloads all my mail into Thunderbird. Like many of my colleagues on our listserv, I don't have the time surf web boards, hoping to see a relevant discussion. The e-mailing forum posts is an excellent way to make efficient use of limited time. I am not going to log-in to Moodle.org or another forum just to read forums -- I only login when I want to comment to a post. The same goes for my classes. The volume of posts generated by my students is not the same as Moodle.org or AMTA, but again, seeing a student's post in my inbox is the reminder to log in to the course. For the professional organization, why not keep the listserv you ask? Currently we create compilations of discussions that Modeling teachers find useful. Doing that is time consuming and onerous for the person who does it. If someone changes a message title slightly, a new thread is started, forcing someone to sift through every message to add to the compilation. By responding to an e-mail (reply to post) on the forum, it forces someone to keep on that thread, even if the message subject changes a bit. From the amount of posts we receive asking for unsubscribing, I suspect quite few people on the listserv do not know how to log into the Listserv server at the list hosting university (which is most likely not be the university where they were trained) and then change subscription settings between digest and individual posts, and fewer people, if any, search for archived posts on a particular topic. Moodle provides a good way to archive the discussion using forums - and an easier search function than a listserv. I know that several folks would like to respond by e-mail as well -- but I do want them to see the site and use it (!) as well as the discussions.

ResponsesInList.Text: I discovered a simple solution to extend the time of editing.  Do the following (ver. 8.1+): 1. Open moodle/administration/settings/security.html in suitable editor.  I used Dreamweaver 4.0. 2. Revise last line of the array as follows: get_string('configmaxeditingtime','admin'), 2700, array(60 => get_string('numminutes', '', 1), 300 => get_string('numminutes', '', 5), 900 => get_string('numminutes', '', 15), 1800 => get_string('numminutes', '', 30), 2700 => get_string('numminutes', '', 45), 7257600 => get_string('numminutes', '', 120960)))); Note: I chose 7257600 seconds (=120960 minutes) because this equals 12 weeks.  Any suitable time period can be chosen. 3. Save and PUT security.html into moodle files using a ftp transfer. 4. Open up your Moodle sites and log on as "Administrator."  Go to the Site Administration/Security/Site Policies.  Find the "Maximum time to edit posts" and select "120960" within the drop-down selection box.  Go to the bottom of the page and "Save Changes." Having done this, participants can now edit their posts for 12 weeks.  At the Catherine of Siena Virtual College, classes can run up to 10 weeks. The extra two weeks enables participants to edit/delete their material during the two weeks following the end of class. From that point onward, materials become the property of the College and can be used to promote the course for forthcoming participants/students.  For details, see http://www.catherinecollege.net/moodle/mod/resource/view.php?id=139 Aaron

Click on the link to the student role. 3. Click on the Edit button. 4. Scroll down to Rate posts and tick the allow radio button (the second column). Thanks, Art

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: I want Forum Ratings to allow Peer feedback!
ResponsesInList.Text: That should work as long as the forums "Allow posts to be rated" (by default, students are not allowed to rate posts even when this box is checked in the forum settings). Then all Students will be able to rate all posts in all forums in all courses in which they are enrolled, as long as those forums "Allow posts to be rated." Unfortunately, you really wouldn't want to do this, since you almost certainly want to grant this permission on a course-by-course, forum-by-forum, and student-by-student basis. Also, you want the teacher to be in control of policy, not the admin. A better solution: cajole/bribe the admin to create a role "CanRatePosts" that turns on a single permission. Then teachers can assign this role to selected students in selected courses or even in particular forums. The flexibility comes from the ability to mix in the permission with other roles in different contexts. I always say "Assign, don't override." But the admin needs to create the role, which is a problem. Roles don't scale. See discussions on this, e.g., this one .

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Students still can't post on Front Page forums V1.8
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Frank, By "course default forum" I assume you mean the news forum. This is a special forum which, as you've found, students are not allowed to start discussions or post replies. Please see docs.moodle.org/en/News_forum for more details. Regarding my previous suggestions: Assign users the front page role of student. This does not make all users students in all courses. It only happens if users are assigned the global role of student. Edit the Authenticated user role and allow the capabilities View discussions, start new discussions, reply to posts etc. This method only works for an ordinary forum. To enable students to start discussions and post replies in a news forum, the capabilities add news and reply to news should be allowed. However, please note that another feature of a news forum is that by default, everyone is forced to be subscribed. Allowing students to start discussions and post replies in a news forum can result in a lot of unwanted emails!

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: How to set 'Only teachers can rate posts' in 1.8
ResponsesInList.Text: If, for example, you did it in the course context it would apply to *all* forums in the post. Howard, You are correct. If you want to limit the ability to post in a specific forum, the teacher must override the Student role in that forum context. Now it gets interesting Suppose you (the teacher) want some students to be able to post but not rate and others to be able to rate but not post. You will create two groups and assign to each one of them its own capabilities. But how? You only have one Student role to override in this context, so that's not a solution. For this, you will need two appropriately-permissioned roles, sayCanPost and CanRate. Because only the someone with permission to Do anything (i.e., the admin) can create roles, you must ask the admin to create these roles for you. Then you can assign them to your groups. I call these "mixin roles" because by assigning them to Students, you mix them in with the Student role. Now what if you want some students to be able to post, some to be able to rate, some to be able to view ratings, etc., etc., etc. In general, if an activity has N capabilities that are normally prevented, you will need N mixin roles. Forum has 13 such capabilities, so in the worst case scenario, you will need the admin to create 13 mixin roles for forum alone. From these, a teacher can create 2**13 = 8192 distinct groups.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: How to set 'Only teachers can rate posts' in 1.8
ResponsesInList.Text: To be fair, pre-roles, you couldn't do that at all. Now you *can* even though blood will be coming out of your ears by the time you have worked out how to do it

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: How to set 'Only teachers can rate posts' in 1.8
ResponsesInList.Text: I'm not suggesting that it SHOULD be done this way. A better solution would be to allow others besides admins to create roles. Currently, only admins (i.e., users with moodle/site:config and moodle/role:manage assigned at system level) can create roles. Teachers can only assign and override such pre-defined roles. As a result, there will be many scenarios in which the Teacher must ask the admin to create one or more new mixin roles. This is administrative overhead for the admin, and it doesn't scale (imagine a school with 1000 teachers). Roles would be (a) easier to explain AND (b) more scalable, if users other than admin were allowed to create new roles. The role creation interface for such users would only show those capabilities relevant to the current context, just as we see in the current Override role pages. It would never show any capabilities that the user does not himself possess, preventing users from passing on greater privileges than they themselves possesses in a given context.

ResponsesInList.Text: On the front page and social formats the discussions are listed in an expanded format where you can read the top post of each discussion.  If the post is longer than forum_longpost then it is truncated to the first sane place (eg end-of-sentence) between forum_shortpost and forum_longpost.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moving A Thread from A Discussion to another Location
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Emma, One of the advantages and/or differences between Moodle and some other LMS's - is that you can create as many forums as you want - and each "forum" can take place of what used to be "threads." So, for example, you may want to have a forum in each unit or learning module. And then each of those forums may have just 3-4 threads. I think that's the way to go. --- In WebCT/Blackboard and the like, you often would have a "discussion" forum - where there was just 1 forum and it was full of threads. I pesonally like them broken up and placed among the content of each module/unit so they are more manageable, easier to find, and more connected to the content and knowledge being discussed. Hope this helps, Clark

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moving A Thread from A Discussion to another Location
ResponsesInList.Text: p.s. - the way to do this would be to use the "topic" or "weekly" format for your moodle course, so that you have a listing in the middle of Topics 1-10 or Weeks 1-10 or etc. Then, in each topic/unit/week, you can "add a resource" (such as a web page, text page, a file: DOC, PPT, or directory. Or on the right, you can "add an activity" - which includes forum, quiz, etc... So in each topic/unit/week you can add as many forums as you like, and this way they are split up among the relevant topics/units/weeks. clark

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Archiving and restoring forums
ResponsesInList.Text: Greetings, Philip! I apologize if I am going off in a totally different direction, but it seems to me that you might be coming from Blackboard or some similar software? In this situation, it was necessary to have an archive tool to get many of the threads split off and placed somewhere other than the current ongoing discussion! Otherwise it took a LONG time to load on some connections. Moodle does not really archive discussions in that way. Instead, you simply set up a different forum. You can have as many as you need to get you through the semester and they are presented as an integrated part of the topic (rather than in a completely different place, as in Blackboard). So this allows you to approach forums somewhat differently. Maybe more chronologically and thematically. In moodle, your forum will be backed up if you back up and restore your course. I implemented the MoodleSpeex module, which allowed audio posts to existing forums, but after implementation, any attempt to create a new forum yielded the error, "Could not add a new instance of forum." Implementation required small changes to three forum module files: mod.html, post.html and post.php; and also to the /files/index.php file (see file attached for changes). There was also a field added to the database forum table (mdl_forum). It was defined a ENUM type (params: 'off','on','default') but since I'm using PostgreSQL I had to modify the data type (no ENUM type in Postgre SQL ). I used boolean type, default value of "false". Also changed the code in post.html and post.php from: if($forum->speex != 'off') to if($forum->speex != 'false')

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: No Discussions, but Replies are Allowed
ResponsesInList.Text: I couldn't find it at first, but here it is. Select the forum you want to change settings for, then select the 'Update this Forum' button. There are two tabs, Update and Roles. Select the Roles tab. Then select the Override Roles tab and select the Student role. Select the Prevent radio button next to Start New Discussions to limit students to respond to the initial prompt message.

ResponsesInList.Title: Novice question: Forums vs. Blogs
ResponsesInList.Text: I am a new Moodle user, supporting it for the teachers at my school, and am trying to set up a student-response activity: students read passages in an assigned book, comment on those passages, and respond to ther students' comments, blog -style. But the feature that is called a 'blog' in my version of Moodle doesn't seem to allow for any secondary responses, only original postings, which can be browsed but not reacted to. Should I instead use the Forum function so that students can interact in the way described above, similar to what we're doing here? Does anyone know of a good discussion somewhere of the merits of Moodle Blogs vs. Forums for classroom use?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Novice question: Forums vs. Blogs
ResponsesInList.Text: That is totally something for forums. You can create a Forum for each passage, or for the book. Ask the students to post their thoughts there, and then ask them to respond to, say, at least two other postings in the forum. You can "force" this to an extent through the forum settings. For example, change the forum type to "Q and A forum", and each student will be *required* to enter something reflectively before being able to see any other posts. You can also use grades (either numerical or a scale of your own devising) so that students can get feedback on their thoughts. You can do this yourself if you like, or allow the students to grade each other.

ResponsesInList.Title: Changing the Term 'Forum' to 'Discussion'

Keeping this term would help eliminate a lot of editing of references to 'Dsicussions' in our course material. Thanks Kim

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Changing the Term 'Forum' to 'Discussion'
ResponsesInList.Text: You could edit the 'forum.php' language file, either by going in Language/Language editing in Site administration, or by directly modifying the language file in lang/en_utf8 (or whatever is the folder for the default language). From there you can change the strings relative to 'forum', 'forums', 'modulename', etc into whatever you want them to be. Hope this helps

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Changing the Term 'Forum' to 'Discussion'
ResponsesInList.Text: Julie > You could edit the ' forum .php' language file, CORRECT.- either by going in Language/Language editing in Site administration, NOT CORRECT.- or by directly modifying the language file in lang/en_utf8 (or whatever is the folder for the default language). If you are using Moodle 1.7, the CORRECT way of editing language files is to go (as Admin) to Administration / language / language editing / Edit words or phrases / Click on forum.php / click on switch button (to make a copy of your local modified language file) and finally locate the words you want to change. Directly modifying the language file is NOT RECOMMENDED. Joseph

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Teacher Forum in Moodle 1.7
ResponsesInList.Text: There are 2 ways to setup a "teacher only" forum (or any resource or activity for that matter). The quickest way is to hide the forum from the students and make sure all staff that need access to the forum are assigned the role of teacher in the course. To do this, first turn editing on . Next click the eye icon next to the forum you want to hide. This will close the eye and turn the link grey. The forum will now be invisible to students, but staff will still be able to see it and use it as normal. The disadvantage to this method is the fact that some teachers think because the link is grey/faded it isn't active (either that or they just have bad eye sight!). Alternatively, you can use the new roles architecture in 1.7 to prevent students accessing the forum. However, they will still be able to see the link to the forum (unless you hide it of course). The benefit of this method is that the text is not greyed out and you can tweak permissions for individual roles. To set up the access rules, go to the forum and click the "Update this Forum" button . Next click the "roles" tab followed by the "overrides roles" tab . Under the "Forums" section select prevent for all the permissions and click "Save changes." Hope this helps, Marty

ResponsesInList.Title: Some (not all) emails delivered from forum postings
ResponsesInList.Text: I have looked over previous posts re. Moodle 1.7 and problems with emails getting successfully sent from forums, and I think ours is a different twist: Some, but not all, emails are getting delivered from forum postings (primarily, though I'm not sure exclusively, news and teacher forums). In terms of roles, authentication (which is the only thing we've recently changed, migrating most users to LDAP ), etc. we can find no real pattern among those who do and do not receive emails. We have checked logs on the smtp server , and all appears fine, so it appears to be a Moodle error and not a mailserver condition. This did not happen before with Moodle 1.6.3+. We have manually run cron jobs just to check the output, and in some cases the number of emails apparently sent out is correct though actual received emails are fewer, and in other cases the number of emails apparently sent out is far fewer than should happen. (More info on how specifically the forum code and cron routine send email, or the files we should inspect to review this code, would be appreciated.) It is, in short, one of those random errors that seems impossible to diagnose, other than that we have successfully run hundreds of forums prior to 1.7. We have upgraded to 1.7.1+ to no avail. Btw , I do not believe it is the roles issue some other threads have mentioned, since roles operate in downward contexts (e.g., roles assigned at the course level operate at the course activity [forum] level, and all users clearly have roles at the course level). Would roles in other contexts (e.g., other courses) have any effect? Thanks for your ideas -- Jim P.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Some (not all) emails delivered from forum postings
ResponsesInList.Text: Jim, are you using a dedicated server or are you on shared hosting? I had a similar issue - we're on a shared host (but not for much longer after this debacle!! ) Since mid December 2006, some emails from my Moodle installation have been failing, and we have been receiving a "Mail delivery failed" message saying that the domain /s in question are unrouteable mail domains. Even more puzzling, some emails to the very same domains are making it through. Before mid December (and since 2003) emails have been sent with no problems. After much digging around, I found that this message can be used when an SMTP server has rate limiting in effect. It is not an issue with any one particular email address. It's not a problem with a password either. The email system is working fine for outgoing email unless they are sent in bulk. It occurs when a php script tries to send an email. The "Mail delivery failed" error message saying that the domain/s in question are unrouteable mail domains seems to have a number of possible causes: 1. If an SMTP server has rate limiting in effect, or 2. The server/s I'm attempting to send to is checking my domain for a proper DNS entry and isn't finding it, because: a. the server hosting my domain is not giving the correct/matching address for the domain and itself. b. the DNS entries for my domain and any subdomains are not valid c. The server on the other side is misconfigured. However, as I am getting the same error message intermittently from a number of big and reputable domains, I discounted 2c. Following a number of emails to and from my web hosting company, with me providing them with the technical knowledge I had gleaned on the subject from searching around the web, they told me that the server is set to send up to 300 mails per hour. If more than 300 emails are send in an hour, the emails will bounce. One message from my Moodle could result in up to 500 outgoing emails - so currently every message that I post results in some bounces. I can understand they're trying to prevent spammers, but what I was annoyed about was that they didn't tell me, and applied the limit without advertising it. Also, the error message I received had nothing to do with the "actual" error, causing me hours of pointless troubleshooting. And if this isn't what causing your problem, apologies for making you read throught this very long post

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Some (not all) emails delivered from forum postings
ResponsesInList.Text: System used: Mac OS X Server running on an xserve Moodle 1.7.1+ PHP 5.1.4 MySQL 5.0.19 Hi All, This is Matthew, I am the sys/network admin at Jim's institution. So, I think we have narrowed down the problem to forum_cron or the forum module. Here's the process we used to narrow our focus: 1. Watch logs in campus-wide SMTP server a. only some mail gets to the SMTP server from moodle b. checked which mail was leaving the moodle box, and everything that left the moodle box was sent successfuly through our mail SMTP server 2. Set up a SMTP server on the moodle box in order to watch only moodle SMTP traffic a. execute cron job - note id number of message (and number sent) b. watch to see if messages in SMTP log match number of messages the forum_cron sent out for a particular message id number So far, any message that is sent from cron_forum gets sent out our SMTP server on the moodle box. What we can't figure out is why some forum messages reach all their recipients and some don't? An example is one of our forums have 15 subscribers. Sometimes the cron_forum states that it is sending a message to 13 users and sometimes 3 users... The My SQL user tables look intact, and there is no evidence of people unsubscribing. Just for sake of disclosure, Jim started out having users use email based authentication, and now he is using LDAP, though, this doesn't seem to affect our issue. Anyone have some ideas? Thanks, Matthew

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: ??? ...
ResponsesInList.Text: There's a thread in Quiz Forum about a similar problem ( http://moodle.org/mod/forum/discuss.php?d=12958 ). I think now this problem may be related with the PHP variable named "session.gc_maxlifetime", which controls the interval of the "garbage collector" in php language. I had this variable set to 1440 seconds (24 min). I've increased it now to 14400 (4 hours), restarted apache, and I hope this will fix this issue. This variable is located in /etc/php4/apache2/php.ini (or /etc/php4/apache/php.ini, depending on your version of apache) I don't know why this variable don't change when changing the "sessiontimeout" option in the moodle's admin page. Perhaps Moodle cannot change a global PHP variable because it can affect other php-based web applications in the same server. And 1440 is the default value. I haven't had this problem with moodle 1.4 because I installed it from debian package, and maybe the debian install script set up this variable to 14400 (4 hours), which is the maximum allowed in the "sessiontimeout" option. Unfortunately, when I upgraded to Moodle 1.5 there was no 1.5 package yet, and I had to install moodle by hand. Perhaps this PHP variable remained set to the default value. Can anyone confirm my assumptions? Thanks.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: ??? ...
ResponsesInList.Text: After some days of testing, I can confirm increasing the "session.gc_maxlifetime" variable in /etc/php4/apache2/php.ini solved the problem (at least for me). I've had an opened session more than one hour doing nothing, and with no timeout. I hope this will be useful to others, although this thread is mysteriously dead now...

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Users confirmation
ResponsesInList.Text: Moshe, Two things you can do to achieve your 2 objectives: 1) Select No Authentication in the Admin/Users/Authentication If you choose this option, then there won't be a create account button, login as guest (with the user being able to choose a username and password) which is validated automatically. 2) Allow auto-enroll: In that case, when a user clicks on a course displayed on the main page, he will be prompted to auto-enroll. Obviously, this will work for you if you don't worry about limiting access to only your students.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Users confirmation
ResponsesInList.Text: I understand that auto-enroll is a course setting? Then does a user still need to register to the site and be confirmed first? myalo

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Users confirmation
ResponsesInList.Text: Myalo, This reply will probably show up twice as the session expired while I was answering. When you have specified "No Authentication" in the Users Authentication field, then, there is no create account button on the moodle home page. To be specific, assume you have published a course. On the home page, there will be Available course and under this title, there will be your course visible to all. If a visitor of the page clicks on it, he will be presented with a login page. He can login as guest then. If he uses username and passwords parameters which are not guest/guest, this will be paramount to creating a new guest account with the new parameters. There is no need to confirm them. What the guest account allows to see and do depends on your definition of privileges. For example, if you have specified when creating a course that guest access "option on the course creation page" can access course without a key, then they will have access to the course like any other student.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle Forums - Why not Focus on Course Content and Use PHPBB, VBulletin, etc.
ResponsesInList.Text: One problem with using other forum (or quiz, etc) software, is user confusion due to interface switching. If you've had to support 1000s of users using several different software applications, you'll know what I mean. IMO , this gets to the core idea; why use an LMS at all? Why not use a forum from one place, a quiz tool from another, a content management tool from another vendor/project, yet another project for chat, etc. etc. and loosely couple them all together for authentication? Sounds like a great idea from the point of view of a person who likes to learn numerous different interfaces. Often the majority of users of an LMS are students and faculty who often do not want to have learn different interfaces to get their work done (and who frequently tell me that they already have too many different interfaces to learn). There has been interesting work by Carl Berger, and others, looking at early adopters (willing to spend time learning different software applications, forgiving of bugs and mistakes) vs. the early majority, who tend more to want a single, simple system that is 'easy to use' and 'does just what I need it to do, and not more'.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle Forums - Why not Focus on Course Content and Use PHPBB, VBulletin, etc.
ResponsesInList.Text: Hi Bill, You have touched the heart of Moodle, and its uniqueness, with your question. Let me answer pedagogically, why Moodle will never have an attached forum like phpBB or vbulletin. Moodle is task-based. Not for content delivery. WebCT, Blackboard and countless others focus on content delivery (and some even call themselves LCMS-learning content management systems). Here learning happens via tasks that people do collaboratively, not so much solitary self-studiers interacting with a page of content. Moodle is flexible, so it *can* do content delivery if you want it to, but it is not actually intended to be used that way. The idea of task-based learning or project-based learning is a big discussion that we can get into. In short, task-based learning is focused more on student initiative and student generation of content, the anti-thesis of teacher-selected/designed content and delivery. Moodle interface focuses on topics. Not on tools. Many LMS interfaces have you go to a chat area, a forum area, or a content area--and attach these standalone tools to enter. Moodle on the contrary, lays out a center window of topics (or weeks) that include all kinds of activities (tasks) mixed up with resources and links to achieve those tasks. Thus your forums are not centralized into one single forum area as in phpBB, but sliced up, and spread across the whole interface into specific topic areas that that particular forum applies to. It's incredibly brilliant. And that alone is a cool idea that Moodle can take pride in as a first invention I have never seen elsewhere.

ResponsesInList.Title: Forums are such an intregal part of collaborative learning
ResponsesInList.Text: Just throwing in my thoughts. We are new Moodle users and are so pleased with the Forum module. It is essential for a number of the collaborative activities we use in our classes, such as case studies and team activities. Because it is an integral part of Moodle, there is no confusion for the learner. And, so far so good, it has worked like a charm--in 1.6+, not in 1.7.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle Forums - Why not Focus on Course Content and Use PHPBB, VBulletin, etc.
ResponsesInList.Text: I wonder how the use of RSS feeds will grow with the increased use of desktop/Internet services such as http://www.netvibes.com/ RSS allows you to keep track of Moodle forums (and all sorts of blogs), only visiting when you want to reply or check out the structure of a thread. In a way, Moodle has already relented on 'users see different structures/views' by allowing users to view forums in different modes, and by the option for users to choose their own theme - what you see is not necessarily what she gets. ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle Forums - Why not Focus on Course Content and Use PHPBB, VBulletin, etc.
ResponsesInList.Text: Both of these cause increased support issues in practice, even though they are actually the same UI . For large installs with many non-technical users, I've been asked to 'hack out' the ability to change themes and to show the forum in different views. Fortunately, there was no hacking required for the former and the later is also now configurable based on roles in 1.7+. The importance of a single interface I would say really depends on your stakeholders: are the target users highly technically skilled individuals with plenty of time to learn several different UIs? PS Netvibes certainly looks interesting, I guess another consideration for stakeholders would be whether you want it to be easy for your students to put an MTV feed alongside your course content (I know that for the above mentioned projects this would be an anathema ).

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Moodle Forums - Why not Focus on Course Content and Use PHPBB, VBulletin, etc.
ResponsesInList.Text: Personally as someone who runs a Moodle site on a volunteer basis, I think it is a bit of a pain to try to support users who have different views but the move toward separation of form and content and the supposed push towards personalised learning environments may change users' expectations. Even the 'transformed VLE ' , see Scott Wilson's PLE diagram may not be what users want in a few years - they may want the interactive content to 'come to them' at their desktop rather in an official PLE - i.e. they may control their own PLE. If there really is a shift in control (e.g. increased use of blogs and wikis) then it may not always be about what 'we' want whoever we are. When HE provided access to the Internet, things were different but increasingly students have their own broadband access and can exercise more choice about how they stay in touch with each other and their tutors. Sites like flickr.com, del.icio.us, etc. know how to minimise the learning overhead and they all fit together without big shifts to the user. I now use a link to del.icio.us tag in my Blackboard course (and would also do so if I was lucky enough to us Moodle for my uni course) so that I can update the web links in del.icio.us. I think that the point you make about MTV feeds is misleading. What the student does on their own private desktop (effectively this is what netvibes is) is invisible to you. At the 'course', the teacher would link to appropriate feeds, they just may not all be in Moodle.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Can one explain pros/cons (differences) about moodle forum and phpbb
ResponsesInList.Text: I am no expert on PHPBB but, here are a few things that spring to mind when comparing them. I have never moderated phpbb (only invision). I can tell I am going to miss out a lot of features on both sides. It is often difficult to say when a feature is an advantage or limitation  but I have given my subjective opinion of advantages in pink. And I am not up to date on moodle 1.7 roles. I think that phpbb may have some mass pruning and user management features that I have no idea about. Moodle PHPBB Integrated with the Moodle LMS and all sort of educational functionality (Perhaps there is a hack somewhere to allow the same authentication to be used on both systems but it will not be integrated in the ways outlined below) Posts can be graded via a drop down menu no grading I am aware of Posts can be graded using a custom scale of non numeric strings no grading I am aware of The submission period can be set, such that only posts made within a particular time slot can recieve a grade. no grading I am aware of The grade can be made viewable only the teacher, only the student and the teacher, by everyone in the posters group and the teacher, or by everyone. no grading that I am aware of The grade is integrated into a gradebook with the grades of all the other learning activities . no grading that I am aware of Who is able to grade (no one, only teachers, all users - and more fine grained using roles) can be specified. no grading that I am aware of Forums structed independently of other forums, so rather than being part of one mother forum, forums are part of Moodle courses Forums are part of a big mother forum and seperate installations are required to create completely seperate forums. Users can choose how the forums are displayed (nested, oldest first, threaded) I don't think the choice is given to users. Users can be placed in groups and a group icon is displayed beneath the users icon Users can be placed in groups but there is no group icon (other than a row of stars) User group membership can be alloted via the suse of (secret) enrollment keys provided to users, as well as manually. I am not aware of an enrolment key function in phpbb but see "The number of posts that a user has made can affect the group" below. Forum posts can be set to be invisible between members of different groups. I am not aware of this function. Forum posts can be set to be un-respondable between members of different groups. I am not aware of this function. The html editor is more advanced, alowing table manipulation, GUI generated image embedding, access to shared images. The html editor is pretty basic. Forums can be set up such that each user can create only one thread. I am not aware of this function. Forums can be set up such that posters are not able to see other threads until they have posted their own thread. I am not aware of this function. Forum notification can be made compulsory I am not aware of this function. Teachers can elect to have notifications sent out immediately rather than after an editing cool down period. Notifications are always sent out pretty Posts are filtered with automatic linking to glossary entries, module names, and media players. I am not aware of this kind of flitering in phpbb, but some forums seem to have simlar (e.g. experts exchange forums are filtered to provide links to advertisers). Users can enrol only in forums and recieve all notifications of new threads posted to that forum. This is one of the biggest complaints about the Moodle forums but the only subscribe to forums, in-for-a-peny-in-for-a-pound style may be one of Moodle's most powerful featurers. Users can enroll and recieve notifications on a per thread basis (other than administrators). The fine grained ability of PHPBB is probably often an advantage, but the "inability" to turn off notifications for forums in moodle makes for a much more lively community Not possible but possibly there is a hack Sticky posts which remain at the top of the forum can be created possible Not possible The number of posts that a user has made is displayable below username/avatar Groups (and later roles) can be set manually and the former by enrolment key (see above) The number of posts that a user has made can affect the group that they belong to (novice, average user, expert...) To quote a post one must copy and paste that post. One can choose to respond quoting the previous post. One must post and then edit but the html editor is more WYSIWYG than in phpbb, so the meaning of preview would be unclear. One can preview ones post As far as I know, only administrators can (with the appropriate configuration setting) edit posts indefinately. Users have up to about 2 hours (settable) to edit their posts. Users can be given permission to edit their posts indefinately. Perhaps it is not possible to limit amount of time that users can edit their posts and so either they can or they can not. Only the single post to which one is responding is displayed. The whole thread is displayed in rerverse order below the response, to that one can look back through all the posts in the thread as one writes ones response. I don't think that this can be done (but inventive use of roles or groups may be able to achieve it) Threads can be closed but left visible. Threads only have titles but: This is a subtitle -- can be used. Threads have subtitles There are no signatures but one can paste on it. Users can set a signature which is automatically appended to all their posts. A lot more could be added to the above list. There are a lot of features that Moodle and phpbb have in common such as... Authentication Site/forum policy disclaimers Searching (by title, forum, user, etc - perhaps moodle allows more fine grained searches) Attachments Moving threads

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: No reply button
ResponsesInList.Text: Don't get a button after their reply editor, or don't get the option to click Reply at the end of the post they are reading? In the latter case you will most likely find that the post was not made to a group. For example, a teacher in two groups must select which group they are in when they post so that that group can reply to it. To have the same discussion apply to multiple groups you must create it multiple times. If you post to no group, all groups can see it but no one can reply. I'm not sure if this is intentional or a bug. This only applies to teacher/admin posts who are in multiple groups - a student automatically posts to their group as would a teacher in only one group. Visible and seperate only determines whether students can see a posts posted under a different group. When in group mode you should see something like this: Discussion Started by Group Replies Unread Last post Missing Content James Ballard staff 2 0 James Ballard Mon, 9 Oct 2006, 01:45 PM Notice the third column is Group - this specifies who can reply, so in this instance only someone in the staff group could reply. A blank group means no one can reply. Visible would let the other group "students" see these posts but not reply, however we use seperate so the "student" group would not even see this discussion.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Installation problem
ResponsesInList.Text: Hello Shyamala, The config file in the moodle folder is where you tell moodle where your database is, and how to connect to it. Bottom line is that if you have MySQL installed correctly, and you have it running (remember, some of the install packages require that you manually start MySQL. Others you can start by clicking on the xampp control panel). and you have set up an empty database ready to receive your Moodle site and you have specified the correct path to the database and you have set the username and password correctly then moodle will be able to connect to the database unless it is being prevented by a firewall or anti-virus software. The other possibility is that some other service may be already listening on the port that MySQL needs to use, and is blocking it. How do your settings compare to these: $CFG->dbtype = 'mysql'; $CFG->dbhost = 'localhost'; //use this if the database is running on the same machine as your moodle installation. Otherwise, you must specify the full path to wherever the database lives. $CFG->dbname = 'moodle'; (assuming this is what you called it) $CFG->dbuser = 'your_username'; (whatever username you configured. The default is 'root', and this is what it will be unless you have changed it. $CFG->dbpass = 'your_password'; The default is blank, no password, and this is what it will be unless you changed it. If you are testing or working on the localhost or a secure LAN, you could temporarily and briefly disable your firewall and your anti-virus, and see if you can connect then. You have managed to get Apache and PHP up and running, so it is safe to assume that MySQL is all right too. It is just a matter of figuring out what is preventing moodle from connecting to the database. Matt

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Installation problem
ResponsesInList.Text: Hello Shyamala, Although using IIS would not be most people's first choice, it seems you have a working server , capable of running php scripts. You also say you have created a database ready for Moodle. All that remains is to tell moodle where that database is and how to connect to it. If MySQL is installed on the same machine on the server, then "localhost" should work in the settings. I don't think you have to link your database to your IIS. All you have to do is tell Moodle where and how to connect to the database. If you are sure the database is running, and you are using the correct username and password to connect, all I can think that is preventing this is A firewall Anti-virus software Some other application is already using the MySQL default port, or the default port is blocked. Maybe someone else out there more familiar with setting up Moodle on IIS could offer more suggestions? Once you get that information into your config.php file, all will be well! So, any IIS gurus out there? Regards to all, Matt

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Installation problem
ResponsesInList.Text: Hello Shyamala, I've been doing a little more research on installing and running MySQL on Windows XP Professional. I came across this: Using XP, you need to create a file called my.cnf and save it to the root of your C: drive, in order to indicate where you have installed MySQL. You can create this file in a text editor like notepad, and it has 3 lines: [mysqld] basedir = c:/mysql/ datadir = c:/mysql/data/ The above file assumes you installed MySQL into the root c folder. If you installed it elsewhere, you need to put in the correct file path. Save this file as my.cnf and make sure you put this name with double quotes around it in the notepad save as dialogue box. If you don't do this, notepad puts a ".txt" appendage on to the file. Then you can hit the Ctrl + Alt + Delete keys to bring up the windows task manager. Hit the Processes tab, and click once on the Image Name column to sort it alphabetically. Scroll down to the m's and hopefully you will see something like mysqld-nt.exe running. Other than all these ideas, if it still doesn't work, all I could suggest is that you uninstall and delete all your current attempted installation from your system and also uninstall IIS. Then go to the Moodle site and download one of the complete packages like xampplite or xampp. I run Windows XP and I downloaded and used the Moodle latest with xampp. The whole thing "jumped" on to my machine and has been running fine since. Let us know how you get on, Matt

ResponsesInList.Title: Increased options for grading forum posts
ResponsesInList.Text:
I would be interested in seeing if other Moodlers would find it useful
to have more options with the grading of forums. Currently, Moodle
simply takes the average of the ratings that a teacher gives and uses
that as the grade for a student. I like to encourage quality not
quantity and would find it helpful to have an option to choose the max
rating. Others have suggested making it total or even just counting the
number of posts. For the time being, I would like to see MDL-3942 worked
on such that the teacher can choose for each forum whether they want
max, min, average, count, or sum used for grading. I think this would
greatly increase the ways that forums could be used in a classroom
setting. I welcome any feedback, support, comments, concerns, etc.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Increased options for grading forum posts
ResponsesInList.Text: Voted for MDL-3942 , Anthony... I was suprised to see it categorized as "trivial." -- Art

ResponsesInList.Title: I'm not sure how your grading scheme should work
ResponsesInList.Text: If you choose max rating how do you account for a student who posts one excellent contribution in the begining of the course and then silence forever? Surely quantity plays a role here at least to some extent as it reflects the student's commitment to the discussion. Furthermore, it is not merely the quantity but also its dispersion over the discussion period. It seems to me that we will need a highly sophisticated scheme for covering all these evaluation aspects if we go by individual message ratings, and I doubt that such a scheme is feasible.

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: I'm not sure how your grading scheme should work
ResponsesInList.Text:
The way that I use a forum discussion is for focused conversations
about a particular theme that does not cover the length of a course.
For example, we just finished watching a film and I had one forum
discussion for the first day of the film and another separate forum for
the end of the film. As a result, I really do expect only one
substantial reply per student as a minimum while allowing them to make
less substantial comments based on what they read. Ideally, I suppose
that I would have a way of rating their ability to contribute to the
conversation but this simple rubric of mine seems to work. As you can
see, there are multiple ways to use the forums and I would like to see
a simple option for how the grade is determined. It would just be a
matter of doing a case statement based on the grading method. There are
times like you describe where you would want an average of the ratings
and others like how I use it where you would want a maximum. Other
teachers may want to allow for the grades to accumulate or maybe even
use the minimum to encourage only more sophisticated replies.
Essentially what I am advocating for is to increase the flexibility
given to the teacher to include not only average (as currently defined)
but also max, min, count, and sum. I think this adds flexibility
without a great deal of sophistication.

ResponsesInList.Title: Thanks. That clarifies some of the issues I'm concerned with
ResponsesInList.Text: I'm definitely not against flexibility. What I find interesting are the various ways for applying pedagogical preferences to current or future features (or vice versa). Here is another question. If these are focused conversations and you require only one substantial contribution, why is it important to rate the secondary contributions? What happens if you don't rate these secondary contributions? Will the grade be lower because it accounts for non-graded secondary contributions by calculating an average?

ResponsesInList.Title: Re: Thanks. That clarifies some of the issues I'm concerned with
ResponsesInList.Text:
I am amazed at how flexible Moodle is and how well is handles so many
different teaching methods. AFAIK , the average is of only the rated
posts. If I could remember which students had already submitted a
substantial reply I could opt to not rate the secondary contribution;
however, I find it better to let the students know the value of each
post. That way, if a student thought he made a substantial contribution
and sees that it was not sufficient or what he had hoped for he can go
back in and try again. The reality is that I often do not remember
which students have submitted and which have not so scoring each post
is easier for me.
